planting.note: Plant bare-root or container grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; this far-northern cultivar tolerates severe Baltic winters better than most Western European apples.

directions: Talvenauding was raised at Estonia's Polli Horticultural Research Centre from an Åkerö × Streifling Herbst cross made in 1946 and officially registered in 2001, becoming one of the longest-storing dessert apples in the Estonian breeding program. The medium, strongly ribbed fruit has greenish-yellow skin striped with brownish red and firm, juicy, greenish-white flesh with a spicy, subacid flavor that improves after a few weeks in storage. Pick while the ground color is still green rather than waiting for full yellow, since the fruit keeps from November into March when cellared cool. Trees are winter-hardy, moderately vigorous with a tidy round-topped habit, bear young, and show good general disease resistance, making this a dependable choice for short, cold growing seasons.
sources: Sordivaramu.ee (Estonian University of Life Sciences fruit cultivar database)
Agronomy Research (Estonian University of Life Sciences)
Polli Horticultural Research Centre

planting.note: Plant certified seed tubers after soil has warmed and danger of hard frost has passed; Piret was bred for short, cool Baltic growing seasons and does not need a long warm stretch to finish.

directions: Piret was released by Estonia's Jõgeva-based crop research institute (now the Estonian Crop Research Institute) as a medium-maturity table variety, carrying the Rpi-R1 gene for strong late blight resistance along with resistance to the golden potato cyst nematode (Globodera rostochiensis). Tasting panels in Estonian trials have repeatedly rated its flavor as pleasant, and the tubers hold a consistently high proportion of marketable size across different growing sites even though raw yield runs lower than newer high-output cultivars. Hill the rows as plants emerge and keep soil moisture even through tuber set to make the most of its naturally modest yield. Because of its built-in nematode and blight tolerance, Piret is a useful choice for home gardeners replanting potatoes on the same ground where those pests have been a recurring problem.
sources: Estonian University of Life Sciences (Agronomy Research / cultivar trial literature)
Estonian Crop Research Institute (ECRI) variety records
potatopro.com Estonia market profile

planting.note: Plant certified seed tubers once soil is workable and frost risk has passed; Maret is one of the earliest-finishing Estonian table cultivars, bulking tubers within about 80 days.

directions: Maret is an early-maturing Estonian table potato developed by the same Jõgeva-based breeding program that produced Piret, reaching harvestable size in roughly 80 days while posting the highest yields among early cultivars in multi-site Estonian trials. It has shown notably slower late blight progression in the field than many other early varieties, giving growers a longer practical harvest window before foliage decline forces an early dig. Because it finishes so quickly, Maret suits short-season gardens or a first early crop ahead of a longer-season main-crop potato planted in the same bed. Dig for fresh eating once the plants begin flowering, or let the vines die back fully for a slightly larger storage harvest.
sources: Agronomy Research (Estonian University of Life Sciences) potato cultivar trial publications
Estonian Crop Research Institute (ECRI) variety records

common_name: Bidi 17 Durum Wheat (Algerian Landrace-Derived Heritage Wheat)

planting.note: Direct sow in autumn in a dry-farmed or low-rainfall climate; Bidi 17 was selected out of early-20th-century North African durum landraces for drought tolerance and performs best where summers are hot and dry.

directions: Bidi 17 traces to a 1930s selection out of the Oued Zenati population, itself drawn from the older North African Bidi landrace complex long grown across Algeria, and it has remained a reference genotype in Algerian durum wheat breeding and drought-tolerance research ever since. The tall-strawed plant carries large, weak-yellow-index grain typical of traditional durum landraces rather than modern short-strawed cultivars, and in root-trait and germplasm studies it has repeatedly been singled out among widely grown Algerian landraces for strong early drought tolerance. Grow it as a dry-farmed, low-input wheat on marginal or water-limited ground rather than a high-fertility bed, since that is the stress environment the landrace was selected to handle. Harvest when stems and heads have fully dried, and mill or use threshed grain for semolina rather than eating it fresh.
sources: ResearchGate/Agronomy journal literature on Algerian durum wheat landrace genetic diversity
MDPI Agronomy — Durum Wheat Seminal Root Traits within Modern and Landrace Germplasm in Algeria

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Nour needs a warm, frost-free citrus climate and is the clementine selection most closely tied to Morocco's Berkane growing region.

directions: Nour arose as a bud mutation of the older clementine cultivar Cadoux, found in Morocco around 1962 and initially marketed abroad under the name Sunerine before growers settled on Nour in the early 1990s. It is now the clementine most strongly associated with the Berkane growing district at the foot of the Beni Snassen mountains, a region whose clementines carry Moroccan geographic-indication recognition for their balanced sugar-acid flavor and perfumed aroma. Fruit is medium-sized, round, with a slightly rough, easily peeled reddish-orange rind and juicy, seedless pulp in isolated plantings, ripening in late January to early February and not holding well once mature on the tree. Plant only grafted stock in full sun on deep, well-drained soil, and pick promptly at color break rather than leaving fruit to hang, since over-mature Nour fruit declines quickly in quality.
sources: Citrus Variety Collection (UC Riverside)
Moroccan citrus trade/IGP documentation (SODEA, Berkane IGP producer sources)

common_name: Djebba Bouhouli Fig (Tunisian AOC Mountain Fig)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring after frost in well-drained soil in full sun; Bouhouli is the dominant fig of Tunisia's Djebba mountain village and prefers a mild Mediterranean-type climate.

directions: Bouhouli is the signature fig of Djebba, a mountain village in Tunisia's Beja governorate, and makes up roughly 85 percent of the orchards that earned Figue de Djebba the country's first-ever appellation-of-origin protection for a fruit in 2012. It bears two distinct crops on old and new wood: an early bather harvest in June and July followed by the heavier karmous main crop in August and September, with fruit that is flattened, averages around 55 grams, and shows a purple skin streaked with green. The variety's reputation for flavor and limited production area let it command prices well above ordinary figs, and it is exported fresh to European and Gulf markets during its short season. Grow in full sun on well-drained, rocky or hillside soil typical of its native terraced plantings, and expect a long-lived, drought-tolerant tree once established with low water needs outside of fruit swell.
sources: pampat.tn — Figues de Djebba AOC / Guide des bonnes pratiques de production des figues à Djebba

Wikipedia — Geographical indications in Tunisia

common_name: Haouzia Olive (INRA Moroccan Dual-Purpose Clonal Selection)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Haouzia is a Moroccan clonal selection bred for high, steady yield and strong disease tolerance.

directions: Haouzia is one of two olive cultivars (alongside Menara) released by Morocco's National Institute of Agronomic Research from clonal selection within the Picholine Marocaine population, aimed at improving on that variety's heavy bearing swings. It carries somewhat larger fruit than Menara, around 3.3 to 5 grams each, with an oil content near 24 percent of dry matter and notably high, fast-starting productivity reported up to 60 kilograms of fruit per mature tree. Growers value it for strong resistance to olive leaf spot and useful tolerance of both olive knot and drought, plus a reduced tendency toward the extreme on-off cropping common in older Mediterranean olive varieties. Use it, like Menara, as a dual-purpose tree for oil or green-cured table olives, planted in full sun on well-drained soil with a compatible pollinizer nearby for best fruit set.
sources: International Olive Council — World Olive Catalogue (Haouzia)
INRA Morocco olive variety evaluation literature

common_name: Menara Olive (INRA Moroccan Oil-Type Clonal Selection)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Menara is a Moroccan oil-focused clonal selection named for INRA's historic olive germplasm collection at Menara, near Marrakech.

directions: Menara was selected by Morocco's National Institute of Agronomic Research from within the Picholine Marocaine population and takes its name from INRA's olive germplasm collection established at Menara, near Marrakech, in 1927. Its fruit runs smaller than its sister selection Haouzia, about 2.5 to 4 grams, but presses out a slightly higher oil content near 40 percent of dry matter with oleic acid levels around 72 percent, making it primarily an oil cultivar rather than a table-olive type. Trees produce comparably heavy crops of up to roughly 60 kilograms per mature tree with a moderate alternate-bearing tendency, and have shown useful partial tolerance of Xylella fastidiosa infection in regional trials. Grow in full sun on deep, well-drained soil with a compatible pollinizer, and press fruit for oil once color has turned from green through purple for the balance of yield and quality favored in Moroccan oil production.
sources: International Olive Council — World Olive Catalogue
INRA Morocco olive variety evaluation literature
sapiama.com Menara cultivar profile

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost in deep, well-drained, alkaline soil; Mateur is Tunisia's leading pistachio cultivar and needs a compatible male pollinator blooming at the same time.

directions: Mateur, selected in northern Tunisia and named for the town of the same name, has become the backbone of Tunisia's pistachio industry, planted far more widely than any other cultivar in the country over the past several decades. Its nut is elongated and medium-sized with a greenish-yellow shell and good natural dehiscence (shell splitting) at maturity, and the kernel runs greener in color than the widely grown American standard Kerman. It flowers very early in the season and matures correspondingly early, typically being harvested in mid-to-late August, two to four weeks ahead of Kerman, and shows a comparatively low rate of blank, unfilled nuts. Like other pistachios it demands a long, hot, arid summer and substantial winter chill in deep, well-drained, alkaline soil, performing poorly in humid climates, and needs a compatible male pollinizer planted nearby for a commercial nut set.
sources: Pomological and physical attributes of pistachio (Pistacia vera L.) varieties grown in west-central Tunisia (jnsciences.org)
